transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's nice to meet you too. I guess what brings me in today is... well, it's getting to be a real problem at work, and I've been doing this a long time, you know? I'm a construction manager, been in the business for years, worked my way up. You'd think by now I'd have a handle on things, but lately—or maybe it's always been this way and it's just catching up to me because the projects are bigger now—I just can't seem to hold my focus when it really matters. 

Like, I'll be standing there, starting a safety briefing with the crew in the morning, or sitting down to review a set of plans, and I go into it telling myself, "Okay, pay attention, this is important, you need to catch everything." And I try, I really try hard to just lock in. But I swear, within a few minutes, maybe even less, my mind is completely gone. I'm suddenly thinking about the concrete delivery that's late, or that framing issue on the third floor, or whether the electrician is going to show up tomorrow. It's like my brain just jumps to three other job problems all at once. And while my mind is off running in a dozen different directions, the guy in front of me is still talking, or I'm still staring at the blueprint, but I'm not actually taking any of it in. Then later, I realize I completely missed things—important things, things I know for a fact I should have caught if I was just paying attention like a normal person. It's embarrassing, honestly, and it's starting to cost us time, which in my line of work means money. I just... I don't know why I can't just stay on track for five minutes when I need to.
Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, did you struggle with these same kinds of focus and attention issues back then, or is this something that only started happening more recently?

Oh, man. No, it's definitely not new. Not at all. If you ask my mom, she’d probably just sigh and shake her head, because even way back in elementary school—I'm talking like, second, third grade—it was already a whole big thing. 

My teachers were constantly pulling my parents in for these parent-teacher conferences. I actually remember my third-grade teacher, she ended up moving my desk right up next to hers because I just... I couldn't stay in my chair. It was like the chair was on fire or something, you know? I'd be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or looking out the window at the playground, or just wandering over to talk to somebody in the back row. And the talking! I was always, always getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I'd just blurt things out. A thought would pop into my head and I wouldn't even think to raise my hand, I'd just say it right over whatever the teacher was trying to explain to the class. 

And then there was the homework situation, which was just a complete disaster. My parents would get so frustrated because I would literally lose my homework all the time. I'd do a worksheet at the kitchen table, shove it in my backpack—which was basically this black hole of crumpled papers and old permission slips—and by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Poof. And on the rare days I actually had the paper in front of me, I’d just ruin it anyway because I never, ever read the instructions. I'd just glance at the first couple of words, think, "Yeah, yeah, I got it," and just speed through the whole thing. I was always rushing. I just wanted to get it done so I could go do something else, but then I'd get the paper back covered in red ink because I completely misunderstood what I was supposed to be doing before I even started. 

So, yeah... it's been like this my whole life, really. It just didn't matter as much when I was nine and the worst thing that happened was I got a bad grade on a spelling test. But now, if I rush through directions on a site plan, or if my mind wanders while we're talking about load-bearing walls, you know, the consequences are a lot heavier. But the way my brain works? That's always been exactly like this. Just always rushing, always blurting things out, always losing things...
